Report the wall-clock time accounting provided by the authors: define "pruning time" as the wall-clock seconds required to obtain the ticket (one-shot FGSM training and pruning) and "training time" as wall-clock seconds to retrain the ticket with PGD; Table 3 reports pruning time $=15{,}462\ \text{s}$ and retrain time $=54{,}090\ \text{s}$ for Ours-40, yielding total time $69{,}552\ \text{s}$. Madry's full PGD training baseline requires $134{,}764\ \text{s}$. Therefore the total wall-clock time for Ours-40 is $0.51\times$ Madry's time (ratio $0.51$), corresponding to a saving of up to $49\%$ of total training time while matching state-of-the-art robustness on the reported attacks and transfer evaluations.
Table 3

State the practical conclusion drawn by the authors: pruning a weakly robust (FGSM-trained) model to get a boosting ticket and then retraining the ticket with full PGD-based adversarial training yields a strongly robust model on WideResNet-34-10 with comparable or slightly improved robust and clean accuracy relative to Madry's baseline, while substantially reducing wall-clock training time (e.g., Ours-40 uses 69,552 s versus Madry's 134,764 s).

Define "one-shot magnitude-based pruning": start from a trained dense model with parameters denoted by $w$ (where $w$ denotes the vector of all model parameters), compute the magnitudes $|w_i|$ for each scalar parameter $w_i$, prune (set to zero and record in a binary mask) those parameters with smallest magnitudes until a target pruning ratio $r$ is reached (where pruning ratio $r$ is the fraction of parameters removed, e.g., $r=0.8$ denotes 80% pruning), and obtain a binary mask $m$ with $m_i=1$ for surviving parameters and $m_i=0$ for pruned ones.

Define "iterative train-prune-reset pruning": initialize and save the original initialization $w^{(0)}$, train the model to convergence producing parameters $w^{(t)}$, prune a fraction of smallest-magnitude weights from $w^{(t)}$, reset surviving weights to the saved initialization $w^{(0)}$, and repeat this train-prune-reset cycle multiple times until the target pruning ratio is reached; this iterative procedure is the method used to find "winning tickets" in prior work.
[5]

Describe the empirical comparison performed by the authors: they obtained pruned sub-networks (tickets) via both one-shot magnitude pruning (single train then prune) and iterative train-prune-reset pruning, then retrained the resulting masked sub-networks from their saved initializations and compared the validation accuracy traces during retraining for VGG-16 and ResNet-18.

Report the empirical outcome of that comparison: the validation-accuracy traces of the tickets obtained by iterative pruning and those obtained by one-shot pruning are visually and numerically indistinguishable in the authors' tracked experiments for VGG-16 and ResNet-18; this evidence is presented as a plot comparing validation accuracy over training steps for both approaches.
Fig. 10

Conclude from the experimental evidence that one-shot magnitude-based pruning followed by resetting the surviving weights to the original initialization and retraining the masked sub-network produces tickets whose boosting effect (faster convergence) and final accuracy are empirically indistinguishable from those obtained by iterative pruning in the reported experiments; therefore, iterative pruning is not necessary to obtain boosting tickets in these experiments.

Start from the upstream result that model capacity controls the boosting effect strength (established earlier): larger capacity (width/depth) increases boosting strength and small models may not support boosting under certain conditions.

Contextualize the prior contradictory claim: a prior work reported that the lottery ticket hypothesis fails to hold in adversarial training (the referenced work), but the authors argue this failure is explained by limited model capacity in the prior experiments.
[29]

Describe the replication and comparison experiment performed by the authors: reproduce the prior small-model setup (a small CNN / LeNet with two convolutional layers) and prune it by $r=80\%$ under adversarial-training regimes; then compare the pruned small model's clean and robust accuracy traces to those of a larger architecture (VGG-16) pruned under the same conditions.

Report the small-model empirical failure: for the small LeNet-like model pruned at $80\%$ under adversarial training, the pruned model degrades into a trivial classifier that predicts a single class for all inputs, yielding validation/test accuracy approximately $11.42\%$ (random-chance-like behavior reported by the authors). This demonstrates that heavy pruning destabilizes the small model under adversarial training causing collapse.
Fig. 9

Report the contrasting large-model success: when applying the same pruning procedure under adversarial training to a larger architecture (VGG-16) the authors recover winning tickets (and boosting tickets) that perform well on clean and robust accuracy; the VGG-16 experiments do not suffer the small-model collapse observed for the LeNet-like architecture.
Fig. 9

Invoke the conceptual explanation provided: adversarial training requires substantially larger model capacity than standard natural training (the authors cite prior work making this point), so pruning a small model under adversarial training removes critical capacity and makes the pruned model unstable and prone to collapse; hence prior negative results on small models are explained by insufficient capacity rather than a universal failure of the lottery ticket hypothesis in adversarial settings.
[22]

Synthesize the conclusion: the empirical failure of prior work to find winning tickets under adversarial training on small architectures is explained by model-capacity limits; experiments that reproduce the small-model collapse and contrast it with successful larger-model pruning support this explanation.
Fig. 9

open_questions.content: Several scientifically meaningful questions remain open and are explicitly acknowledged by the authors. First, the mechanistic cause of the boosting effect is unresolved: it is unclear why certain pruning masks plus the original initialization yield a sub-network whose training trajectory aligns with a projected full-model path and attains faster convergence, and the relationship (or distinction) between boosting tickets and knowledge-distillation-like information transfer is not settled. Second, finding boosting tickets without ever training a full dense model beforehand remains an open problem; the authors note it is "technically not necessary" but do not provide a method. Third, combining boosting-ticket-based epoch reduction with complementary per-epoch acceleration techniques (e.g., methods that recycle gradient computations during adversarial example generation) is proposed as a promising future direction but is not evaluated here. Finally, the limits of the boosting phenomenon across other datasets, tasks beyond image classification, alternative pruning criteria, and stronger or adaptive adversaries beyond the tested PGD/transfer/C&W evaluations are not resolved within this work.
